nameStory: The Sprinkled Locust gets its charming name from the tiny speckles and spots scattered across its body, like someone gently sprinkled pepper or seeds over its surface. This delicate pattern of markings gives it a distinctive 'dusted' appearance that sets it apart from other grasshoppers in New England.
description: The Sprinkled Locust is a medium-sized grasshopper that belongs to the short-horned grasshopper family, meaning its antennae are relatively short compared to its body length. Like other slant-faced grasshoppers, its head has a distinctive angled profile when viewed from the side. These nimble hoppers are brownish or grayish with characteristic speckled markings across their wings and body. They're strong jumpers and can also fly short distances when disturbed.

idTips.label: Speckled Pattern
idTips.description: Look for tiny dark spots scattered across the wings and body like pepper flakes - this sprinkling pattern is the key identifying feature and feels slightly rough to the touch

idTips.label: Slanted Face
idTips.description: The head slopes backward at an angle when viewed from the side, creating a distinctive wedge-shaped profile rather than a rounded face

idTips.label: Short Antennae
idTips.description: Antennae are notably shorter than the body length and feel thick and sturdy - much stouter than the thread-like antennae of katydids

idTips.label: Brown-Gray Coloring
idTips.description: Base color ranges from earthy brown to grayish-brown, providing excellent camouflage against soil and dried vegetation

idTips.label: Wing Length
idTips.description: Wings extend beyond the tip of the abdomen and have a somewhat broad appearance with visible veining patterns

habitat: Sprinkled Locusts prefer open, sunny areas with sparse vegetation including old fields, meadows, and grassy hillsides throughout New England. They're often found in areas with sandy or well-drained soils where grasses and low herbs grow. Look for them in disturbed habitats like roadsides, power line cuts, and the edges of agricultural fields.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet active; eggs overwinter in the soil and begin hatching as temperatures warm in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible, active, and vocal. This is the best time to observe their distinctive speckled pattern and hopping behavior.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active into early fall, mating and laying eggs in the soil before the first hard frosts end their season.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground activity; eggs remain dormant in the soil, protected from freezing temperatures until spring hatching.

funFact: Despite being called a locust, this grasshopper is completely harmless and won't swarm - true locusts are actually a different type of grasshopper that can form devastating migratory swarms, but our gentle Sprinkled Locust prefers to live a quiet, solitary life munching on grasses!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other brown grasshoppers, but the speckled pattern is your best clue - think 'sprinkled with pepper' and you'll remember to look for those diagnostic spots that other similar grasshoppers lack.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'locust' in grasshopper common names often causes confusion since biblical locusts were actually swarming grasshoppers from different species entirely. Our New England 'locusts' like this one are peaceful, non-swarming grasshoppers that got the locust name from early settlers who applied it broadly to hopping insects.
compareHints: Since this is the only Chloealtis species in New England, compare it to other slant-faced grasshoppers in the region. The Sprinkled Locust's distinctive speckled pattern and broader wings help distinguish it from the more uniformly colored slant-faced species. Its relatively robust build and clear speckling pattern make it one of the easier slant-faced grasshoppers to identify with confidence.
